title_original: «Il futuro dell’architettura è ancora un disegno»: parola di Peter Cook, fondatore di Archigram
editorial_title_zh: «建筑的未来依然是一张图纸»：Archigram 创始人彼得·库克（Peter Cook）如是说
editorial_excerpt_zh: 90岁的 Archigram 创始人仍在用画笔勾勒城市与建筑。在都灵的 Utopian Hours 活动上，他分享了为什么他更青睐远见而非乌托邦，以及为什么即使是最大胆的构想也必须面对现实。文章《建筑的未来…

article_text:
«Utopia? No, grazie». L’idea che i maestri dell’architettura dispensino pillole di saggezza come piacerebbero a noi non supera quasi mai la prova delle interviste. Succede anche con Sir Peter Cook : parli al progettista britannico che negli anni Sessanta fondò Archigram , contribuendo a liberare l’architettura dalla dittatura degli edifici immobili e immaginando città che camminano, e, quando gli chiedi perché abbiamo smesso di coltivare il sogno, risponde sostanzialmente che preferisce parlare d’altro. Il che ha qualcosa di bizzarro, se pensiamo che siamo a Torino, a Utopian Hours, il festival dedicato al futuro delle città che lo ha invitato a tenere una masterclass, mentre una mostra dei suoi disegni, The City is a Garden , a cura di Claudia Pasquero ed ecoLogicStudio, ne celebra l’immaginazione.

Cook, soprannominato all’epoca con i colleghi di Archigram il Beatles dell’architettura radicale, a ottobre ha compiuto novant’anni. E ha poca voglia di farsi trasformare in un monumento all’utopia. Preferisce parlare di progetti, di problemi, di soluzioni. E di quello che accade quando le idee incontrano la forza di gravità.

Il cappello e la città impossibile per Peter Cook

Per esempio, The Line, la città lineare lunga 170 chilometri immaginata nel deserto saudita nell’ambito del progetto Neom, il gigantesco esperimento urbanistico che prometteva di rivoluzionare l’idea stessa di abitare. Cook è stato coinvolto nella progettazione, insieme a molti altri architetti di fama internazionale. «A Londra ci hanno lavorato praticamente tutti», scherza. A lui è toccato studiare una parte residenziale, ragionando sulla frammentazione delle unità abitative e sulla loro distribuzione lungo due fronti. Il problema era integrare gli edifici nel paesaggio, racconta, rispettando al tempo stesso la richiesta di svilupparli molto in altezza, su sezioni estremamente strette. Una combinazione che produceva difficoltà strutturali enormi. Gli chiedo se fosse sbagliata l’idea di partenza o se lo fosse perché tecnicamente irrealizzabile. Cook risponde con un gesto. Si tocca il cappello, se lo sistema sulla testa e spiega che, se qualcuno gli chiedesse di portarlo sempre più in alto, arriverebbe un momento in cui non potrebbe più indossarlo. L’architettura funziona allo stesso modo: puoi spingere una forma oltre ogni convenzione, ma devi ancora poterla usare. Una lezione sorprendente, pronunciata da un uomo che ha passato la vita a disegnare città impossibili. E che ricorda come The Line sia stata presentata anche a Venezia. «Ma pure Venezia è surreale», aggiunge, lasciando aperta una questione: quali impossibilità siamo disposti ad accettare, e perché?

Visionari, con i piedi per terra

Gli chiedo allora che cosa significhi essere visionari. La risposta è fulminea: «Io, noi siamo visionari!». Subito dopo arriva la precisazione che vale l’intera conversazione: la visionarietà deve integrarsi nella realtà. Anzi, aggrapparcisi. Meglio questo che l’utopia, parola sufficientemente elastica da consentire a chiunque di immaginare qualsiasi cosa senza doversi preoccupare troppo delle conseguenze. Cook non sembra avere molta pazienza con l’utopia quando diventa un lasciapassare per ignorare i vincoli del mondo reale. Gli interessa una visionarietà capace di spingere la realtà oltre i propri limiti senza perdere il contatto con la possibilità di costruire. Come ha spiegato di recente, le architetture che immagina sono «possibili, o quasi possibili, ma soprattutto non deliberatamente impossibili».

Ripensando ad Archigram, il ragionamento acquista un significato particolare. La celebre Plug-In City del 1964, con le sue unità intercambiabili, nasceva da una domanda concretissima: perché gli edifici devono durare più delle esigenze di chi li abita? Dietro le immagini fantascientifiche, c’era una critica al funzionalismo e alla rigidità della città moderna. Il futuro serviva a interrogare il presente.

Il diritto di giocare

Nella masterclass presso La Centrale Lavazza, location della decima edizione del festival torinese del citymaking, Cook organizza la propria esperienza attraverso una griglia di temi: paesaggio, città, interni, padiglioni. Quest’ultima categoria gli è particolarmente cara. Il padiglione è il territorio del gioco, della sperimentazione, della libertà di tentare qualcosa senza l’obbligo di trasformarlo immediatamente in modello universale. A novant’anni, Cook continua a considerare il gioco un formidabile motore dell’architettura.

Da oltre sessant’anni affida al disegno il compito di esplorare territori nei quali l’architettura costruita fatica ad avventurarsi. Disegnare gli permette di mettere insieme ciò che nella realtà tende a rimanere separato, di forzare le proporzioni, inventare geografie e studiare le conseguenze di un’intuizione. «Il mio lavoro riguarda l’immaginazione che gioca», racconta. Nei suoi disegni convivono elementi belli, inquietanti e questioni architettoniche estremamente serie, spesso accostati in modi imprevedibili. Compaiono città attraversate da strutture monumentali, edifici che sembrano crescere come organismi, case nascoste nei pendii, paesaggi nei quali vegetazione e costruzioni si contendono lo spazio. Il disegno conserva per Cook una libertà che il rendering fotorealistico tende a sacrificare: può mostrare qualcosa che ancora non esiste senza dover fingere che sia già stato costruito. Lui dice di no, ma a noi piace pensare che sia la nuova, ennesima utopia.

article_text:
Van Gogh erzielte am Mittwochabend bei Sotheby’s einen Rekordpreis. Die Ergebnisse der Auktionen belegen einmal mehr den Boom der Auktionen aus Einzelbesitz

Sammlungen aus einer Hand haben derzeit Hochkonjunktur auf dem Kunstmarkt. Am 18. November versteigerte Sotheby’s New York zwölf Gemälde aus der argentinischen Sammlung Blaquier-Arrieta, die seit 1975 nicht mehr öffentlich zu sehen gewesen waren. Der Schätzwert lag bei rund 450 Millionen Dollar. Für Vincent van Goghs "Blühende Kastanienbäume" (1890) wurden 190,4 Millionen Dollar erzielt – deutlich mehr als der bisherige Auktionsrekord des Künstlers von 117,2 Millionen Dollar. Die Auktion war von Sotheby’s mit einer Garantie in unbekannter Höhe abgesichert worden.

"Sammler erkennen, dass sie möglicherweise sehr lange keine vergleichbare Gelegenheit mehr bekommen werden", sagt Megan Fox Kelly, eine New Yorker Beraterin, die mit Nachlässen von Sammlern und deren Erben arbeitet, gegenüber Monopol. Doch was sagt diese Auktionswoche mit ihrem Schwerpunkt auf Einzelbesitz-Sammlungen über den Kunstmarkt insgesamt aus?

Am 12. November, sechs Tage vor der Auktion, hatten die Erben des Berliner Verlegers Samuel Fischer Sotheby’s über ihren Anwalt Gunnar Schnabel aufgefordert, das Van-Gogh-Gemälde zurückzuziehen. Sie argumentierten, das Bild sei 1936 unter Zwang verkauft worden, wenige Monate nachdem die Familie vor den Nationalsozialisten aus Berlin geflohen war. Am 17. November, dem Vorabend der Auktion, teilte Sotheby’s mit, dass die Familie Blaquier-Arrieta und sämtliche rechtmäßigen Nachkommen von Hedwig und Samuel Fischer eine "für beide Seiten zufriedenstellende Lösung" gefunden hätten . Weder die Bedingungen der Einigung noch die Frage, ob die Erben eine Entschädigung erhalten, wurden bekannt gegeben.

"Blühende Kastanienbäume" erzielte dann einen neuer Auktionsrekord für den Künstler. Den Zuschlag erhielt der New Yorker Händler Bill Acquavella nach einem dreiminütigen Bietergefecht. Alle zwölf Werke aus der Sammlung Blaquier-Arrieta wurden verkauft. Einschließlich Gebühren kamen sie auf 412 Millionen Dollar – knapp unter der Vorabschätzung von 414 bis 462 Millionen Dollar.

38 Prozent des Umsatzes aus Einzelbesitz-Versteigerungen

2025 entfielen laut der Bank of America Private Bank 38 Prozent des Auktionsumsatzes in New York auf Einzelbesitz-Versteigerungen. Zwischen 2015 und 2020 hatte ihr Anteil im Durchschnitt noch bei sieben Prozent gelegen. Das entspricht mehr als einer Verfünffachung. Der Branchennewsletter "Wall Power schätzt den Vorabwert der November-Auktionen auf rund 1,7 Milliarden Dollar. Mehr als 600 Künstler sind vertreten, wobei die zehn teuersten Positionen etwa die Hälfte des Gesamtwerts ausmachen. Doch der scheinbare Boom ist enger begrenzt, als diese Zahlen vermuten lassen.

"Der Markt wird in erster Linie vom Angebot bestimmt", sagt Clare McAndrew, Gründerin von Arts Economics, die den "Art Basel & UBS Art Market Report" erstellt. Wenn mehr Werke auf den Markt kämen, könne dies einen positiven, preistreibenden Effekt haben – das Gegenteil anderer Anlageklassen, in denen ein größeres Angebot oder ein Überangebot die Preise tatsächlich sinken lasse. Fox Kelly sieht ebenfalls keine Überversorgung: "Ich glaube nicht, dass wir zwangsläufig zu viele Sammlungen aus Einzelbesitz sehen. Es ist vielmehr ein Spiegelbild des gegenwärtigen Generationenwechsels."

Der Trend nahm im November 2025 richtig Fahrt auf. Damals machten vier eigens Sammlungen gewidmete Abendauktionen in New York rund 43 Prozent der etwa 2,2 Milliarden Dollar aus, die die drei großen Auktionshäuser in dieser Woche umsetzten. Drei der vier Auktionen waren vollständig ausverkauft. Allein die Sammlung von Leonard A. Lauder erzielte einschließlich Gebühren 527,5 Millionen Dollar. Den Spitzenpreis erreichte Gustav Klimts "Bildnis Elisabeth Lederer" mit 236,4 Millionen Dollar.

Sammlung Lauder, Koons, Schlumberger

In diesem Jahr summieren sich die veröffentlichten Ergebnisse der Sammlung Blaquier, der eigenen Sammlung von Jeff Koons bei Christie’s (rund 100 Millionen Dollar) und des Nachlasses von Agnes Gund (rund 25 Millionen Dollar) auf etwa 575 Millionen Dollar. Die Konzentration ist sogar noch größer: Die Sammlung Blaquier umfasst zwölf Werke, während Lauders Sammlung 2025 mit 24 Losen vertreten war.

Die ersten Ergebnisse fallen unterschiedlich aus. Am 16. November verkaufte Sotheby’s sämtliche 24 Werke aus der Sammlung Theodore und Ruth Baum für insgesamt 109,9 Millionen Dollar einschließlich Gebühren. Einen Abend später erzielte die Einlieferung von Koons bei Christie’s 104,7 Millionen Dollar. Das Spitzenlos, Pablo Picassos "Le Baiser", blieb mit einem Zuschlag von 26,5 Millionen Dollar jedoch deutlich unter der Schätzung von 40 bis 60 Millionen Dollar.

In Paris erzielte die Sammlung Schlumberger bei Sotheby’s am 22. Oktober ohne Garantien einschließlich Gebühren 74,4 Millionen Euro – fast das Doppelte der unteren Schätzung. Claude Monets "Iris" wurde für 50 Millionen Euro verkauft, bei einer Schätzung von 22 bis 30 Millionen Euro.

"Frische, prominente und klar zuordenbare Sammlungen"

"Frische, prominente und klar zuordenbare Sammlungen absorbieren das Angebot gut", sagt Anders Petterson, Gründer des Marktforschungsunternehmens ArtTactic, gegenüber Monopol. Bei Auktionen mit Werken verschiedener Eigentümer sah die Lage anders aus: In London wurden nur 24,3 Prozent der Lose oberhalb der mittleren Schätzung verkauft – ein Rückgang um 12,3 Prozentpunkte gegenüber dem Vorjahr. "Die Nachfrage ist also vorhanden, aber selektiver", sagt Petterson.

Mit dem Wandel des Marktes könnte allerdings auch die Macht großer Sammlernamen schwinden. "Da das Publikum der Sammler globaler geworden ist, lässt sich das Vermächtnis eines Sammlers nicht unbedingt kulturübergreifend übertragen", sagt Alex Glauber, Gründer der New Yorker AWG Art Advisory. "Die nächste Generation von Sammlern verehrt nicht automatisch dieselben kulturellen Wegbereiter."

Fox Kelly differenziert genauer: "Ich würde unterscheiden zwischen einem Aufpreis für ein großartiges Werk, das zufällig aus einer berühmten Sammlung stammt, und einem Aufpreis, der allein dem Namen der Sammlung geschuldet ist." Qualität, Seltenheit und die Nachfrage nach dem Werk eines Künstlers seien weiterhin wichtiger als jeder andere Faktor.

Verschiebung der Segmente

Die Beliebtheit von Einzelbesitz-Auktionen ist nicht die einzige Veränderung auf dem Markt. Auch die Interessen der Käufer haben sich in verschiedenen Segmenten verschoben. Der "Art Basel & UBS Art Market Report 2026" zeigte, dass die Verkäufe impressionistischer und postimpressionistischer Kunst 2025 um 47 Prozent auf 1,8 Milliarden Dollar stiegen. Der Umsatz mit moderner Kunst legte um neun Prozent auf 2,4 Milliarden Dollar zu, wobei fast der gesamte Zuwachs auf Werke über einer Million Dollar entfiel. Die Verkäufe von Nachkriegs- und Gegenwartskunst gingen dagegen um zwei Prozent auf 4,5 Milliarden Dollar zurück. Es war das vierte Jahr in Folge mit rückläufigen Zahlen. Arts Economics bezeichnet zeitgenössische Kunst als "das einzige Segment mit einem erneuerbaren Angebot" – und dennoch ist es gerade dieses Segment, das Verluste verzeichnet.

Woran liegt das? Zum einen ist das Vermögen an der Spitze gewachsen. Das Vermögen der Milliardäre erreichte 2025 laut dem "UBS Billionaire Ambitions Report 2025" mit 15,8 Billionen Dollar einen Rekordwert – ein Plus von 13 Prozent innerhalb eines Jahres. Dem Gesamtmarkt hat dies allerdings nicht gleichermaßen geholfen.

"Rekordpreise wirken sich normalerweise nicht auf weniger bedeutende Werke desselben Künstlers aus. Jedes Bild wird für sich betrachtet", sagt Thomas Seydoux gegenüber Monopol. Der ehemalige Vorsitzende der Abteilung für impressionistische und moderne Kunst bei Christie’s ist heute als privater Kunsthändler tätig.

Wer sind die Käufer?

Wer hinter den Ausgaben steckt, ist weniger eindeutig. "Meiner Einschätzung nach handelt es sich überwiegend um amerikanische Sammler, mit einer gewissen Aktivität aus Asien", sagt Seydoux. "Etablierte Sammler suchen nach dem fehlenden Stück, neue Sammler konzentrieren sich auf ihren eigenen Geschmack. Neue Sammler scheinen Werke bis auf Rekordpreisniveau zu treiben. Dabei geht es eher um individuelle Vorlieben und Geschmack als um Spekulation."

Petterson widerspricht. "Die Indikatoren deuten eher auf eine etablierte Käufergruppe hin, die sich in Sicherheit bringt, als auf eine Welle neuen Geldes." Er verweist auf Christie’s: Bei den Londoner Auktionen im Oktober kamen 59 Prozent der Bieter aus Europa, dem Nahen Osten und Afrika, 31 Prozent aus Amerika und zehn Prozent aus dem asiatisch-pazifischen Raum. Der Anteil asiatischer Bieter war damit niedriger als 2025 und 2024.

Christie’s-Auktionator Adrien Meyer setzte dem nach der Abendauktion zur Kunst des 20. Jahrhunderts am 17. November, die einschließlich Gebühren 627 Millionen Dollar einbrachte, eine andere Beobachtung entgegen. Er sprach von einer "erheblichen Beteiligung aus Asien", wie er sie seit längerer Zeit nicht mehr erlebt habe.

Garantien als Versicherung

Hinzu kommt, dass ein Großteil der Stärke bereits im Vorfeld abgesichert wird. Garantien deckten 2025 laut der Bank of America Private Bank 78 Prozent des Werts der New Yorker Abendauktionen ab. Bei den Londoner Abendauktionen im Oktober zählte Petterson 64 garantierte Lose. Das waren 45 Prozent aller angebotenen Werke und 79 Prozent der Zuschlagssumme – ein "Zehnjahreshoch", das auf einen unsicheren Markt hindeute.

Auch in New York sieht es nicht anders aus: 36 der 75 Lose bei der entsprechenden Christie’s-Auktion waren garantiert, 31 davon durch Dritte. Auktionshäuser übernehmen solche Garantien häufig zunächst selbst und geben sie dann einzeln oder in Paketen an Dritte weiter, erklärt Glauber. "Im Grunde handelt es sich um eine Versicherung. Der Preis dafür ist allerdings, dass sie den breiteren Bieterwettbewerb und die Konkurrenz während der eigentlichen Auktion oft abschwächen."

Für einen Rekordpreis braucht es zwei Bieter – und auf diesem Niveau ist die Luft dünn. Wenn ein Käufer ausfällt, kann das ein Auktionshaus bei einem einzigen Los Dutzende Millionen kosten. Bis zur Einigung am 17. November drohte der offene Restitutionsanspruch genau ein solches Szenario. Wäre einer der Bieter für den Van Gogh abgesprungen, hätte das Bild entweder mit nur einem Gebot den Zuschlag erhalten oder wäre an den Garantiegeber Sotheby’s gegangen.

Vor der Auktion sagte Fox Kelly, sie werde besonders auf die Zahl der gehobenen Bieterkarten achten. "Eine Garantie darf nicht mit tatsächlicher Wettbewerbsnachfrage verwechselt werden. Sie begründet eine finanzielle Verpflichtung, sei es durch das Auktionshaus oder einen Dritten. Was während der Auktion geschieht, ist eine andere Frage", sagte sie. "Die Höhe der Gebote ist ein besserer Indikator für die Tiefe der Nachfrage als die Gesamtsumme der Verkäufe allein."

Neuer Rekord für eine einzelne Auktionsnacht bei Sotheby’s

Der Rekordpreis des Van Gogh beantwortet die Frage der Vorberichterstattung zumindest an der absoluten Spitze des Marktes – jedenfalls mit Blick auf die Preise. Die Gebote legen allerdings nahe, dass die dahinterstehende Nachfrage weniger stark war. Monets "Iris" benötigte in Paris 45 Minuten, um verkauft zu werden, der Van Gogh nur drei.

Laut "Artnet News" waren neun der zwölf Lose aus der Sammlung Blaquier-Arrieta zusätzlich zur Sotheby’s-Garantie durch unwiderrufliche Gebote abgesichert. Das Auktionshaus trug das Risiko also nicht allein. Die meisten Werke wurden mit nur einem Gebot verkauft. Sieben, darunter der Van Gogh, dessen Zuschlag bei 165 Millionen Dollar lag, blieben unter ihren unteren Schätzpreisen. Cézannes "Harlekin", auf 120 bis 150 Millionen Dollar geschätzt, zog lediglich einen Bieter an und erzielte einschließlich Gebühren 111 Millionen Dollar. Damit blieb das Werk deutlich unter dem Auktionsrekord des Künstlers von 138 Millionen Dollar.

Die Einigung im Streit um die Provenienz beantwortete eine engere Frage: Ein Restitutionskonflikt muss eine frische, prominente Sammlung nicht zu Fall bringen – vorausgesetzt, er wird vor Beginn der Gebote beigelegt.

Fox Kelly hatte vorhergesagt, dass die New Yorker Auktionen "viel über das Vertrauen an der absoluten Spitze des Marktes verraten würden, vielleicht aber weniger über die Gesundheit des Gesamtmarktes". Die anschließende Auktion mit Werken verschiedener Eigentümer lieferte eine erste Antwort auf die zweite Frage. Sie erhöhte das Ergebnis des Abends auf insgesamt 777,8 Millionen Dollar – ein neuer Rekord für eine einzelne Auktionsnacht bei Sotheby’s. Die Auktion übertraf die obere Schätzung, 98 Prozent der Lose wurden verkauft. Zudem erzielte sie neue Auktionsrekorde für Mary Cassatt (13,3 Millionen Dollar) und Aaron Douglas: Sein Gemälde "Harriet Tubman" (1931), eingeliefert vom Bennett College, brachte 14,5 Millionen Dollar ein. Die Schätzung hatte bei 2,5 bis 3,5 Millionen Dollar gelegen.

article_text:
Great news: We have a new look! At 17, we're refreshing Hyperallergic 's logo and site design to reflect our growth as a leading source for trusted art reporting and criticism while maintaining our playful, irreverent spirit. Special thanks to our paying members, without whom this makeover wouldn't have been possible.

In other news, pathbreaking museum leader Thelma Golden is stepping down after 21 years at the helm of the Studio Museum in Harlem. Meanwhile, the Old Acropolis Museum in Athens is reopening after a two-decade renovation.

Also today, scholar and curator Anuradha Vikram writes about the value of performance art in today's fractured society and fraught politics, and Staff Reporter Rhea Nayyar speaks with the National Gallery of Art's 78-year-old curator and viral sensation Alison Luchs, or, as the kids call her, the "museum rizzler."

—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

Hyperallergic has a new look!

From the start in 2009, Hyperallergic has been kicking at the doors of the art world status quo, challenging assumptions about what is worthy of investigation and investment, and the supposed neutrality of those decisions. Today, 17 years later, we are no longer a young upstart blogazine but a daily source of trusted news, reviews, and opinions for millions in the art community.

Today, we are excited to introduce the next transformation of this site, with a whole new look, a dynamic homepage, and the third version of our wordmark. | Veken Gueyikian

“Free Lyric” Tells the Story of a Young Black Female Rapper Cancelled for Her “Provocative” Lyrics

Watch the new documentary by BAFTA award-winning filmmaker Cherish ‘Chez’ Oteka on Field of Vision.

News

One year after the Studio Museum in Harlem's long-awaited reopening, Thelma Golden announces her intention to step down after 21 years as the institution's director and chief curator.

After shuttering in 2007 to undergo renovation, the Old Acropolis Museum reopens in Athens, Greece .

Visionary curator and mixed-media artist Tamlin Blake was found murdered in her Riebeek West home in South Africa.

Interview

How Alison Luchs, the “Museum Rizzler,” Became Gen Z’s Goated Art Historian

The National Gallery of Art's 78-year-old Early European sculpture curator and designated baddie gives us the deets on how she became a social media superstar overnight. | Rhea Nayyar

San Antonio’s Centro de Artes Celebrates 10 Years with "Mercado/Material"

Curated by Mia Lopez, 16 artists transform everyday objects into bold explorations of Latinx identity. On view in San Antonio from October 16 through March 7, 2027.

From Our Critics

When a Ceramics Studio Becomes a Stage

In Matthew Lutz-Kinoy’s "The Mud Room," the gallery acts as a site of production. | Phillip Pyle

Jessica Craig-Martin’s Exercise in Name-Dropping

The photographer never asked to be born into her parents’ successful art and social lives. Her observations about the latter taint the former, and the result is a pervasively superficial way of looking at the world. | Olivia McEwan

Opinion

Performance Artists Who Put Their Bodies on the Line

With its emphasis on embodied experience, performance provides a necessary counteraction to cheap political theater and the dissociation and isolation of our fractured, digitized society. | Anuradha Vikram

University of Michigan’s Fully Funded MFA Program Combines Studio Art and Research

Top-ranked, tuition-free MFA program at University of Michigan's Stamps School of Art & Design supports interdisciplinary, research-based practices.

From the Archive

The Story of Surrealism Isn’t Whole Without Gala Dalí

In Surreal , Michèle Gerber Klein asks us to confront the unjust eclipse of Gala’s legacy by that of her husband, Salvador, whose career she brought to fruition. | Hall Rockefeller

article_text:
“ Love Actually ” might be one of the most beloved — if controversial — Christmas classics, but don’t try quoting the film to star Keira Knightley. The actress recently revealed that she actually hasn’t watched the film in decades, so interactions with fans who reference her lines mean “nothing” to her.

“I have not watched ‘Love Actually’ since the premiere, which was when I was 18,” she told Heart . “So, I think I’m the person that knows it the least of anybody. I know that people have a particular look on their face and then they say things to me and I know that means they’re quoting ‘Love Actually,’ but I don’t really know what it is. It means nothing to me.”

Related Stories

CMA Awards Predictions: Expect Ella Langley to Get Everything but Male Vocalist, and Maybe Even That's Not Safe

Taylor Swift to Perform at CMAs for the First Time in 13 Years

While filming, Knightley was just 17 and on set for only a week, which contributed to her inability to recall the script. “It was a week when I was 17, so I don’t remember it really,” she continued. “I mean, I quite like that it has this life, this, such a big life out there.”

In the 2003 film, Knightley plays Juliet, a woman who gets married only to learn that her husband’s best friend is actually in love with her. In a now infamous scene, the friend appears at her door and confesses his feelings using cue cards. The cards read: “Let me say, without any hope or agenda, just because it’s Christmas (and at Christmas you tell the truth) to me you are perfect.”

In 2024, Knightley described the moment as “quite creepy” in an interview with the Los Angeles Times. “The slightly stalker-ish aspect of it — I do remember that,” Knightley said. “My memory is of [director] Richard [Curtis], who is now a very dear friend, of me doing the scene, and him going, ‘No, you’re looking at [Lincoln] like he’s creepy,’ and I’m like, ‘But it is quite creepy.’ And then having to redo it to fix my face to make him seem not creepy.”

When asked if she felt there was a creep factor to the scene while filming it, Knightley responded: “I mean, there was a creep factor at the time, right? Also, I knew I was 17. It only seems like a few years ago that everybody else realized I was 17.”

article_text:
News

National Gallery Singapore to Welcome Chng Hak-Peng as New CEO

CHNG HAK-PENG . Courtesy National Gallery Singapore.

The National Gallery of Singapore (NGS) and Singapore Art Museum (SAM) announced today that Chng Hak-Peng will succeed Eugene Tan as chief executive officer of NGS, effective from January 1, 2027. Tan will step back from his NGS duties at the end of the year to concentrate on his role as SAM’s chief executive officer and director.

Chng brings over 30 years’ experience in Singapore’s arts and culture sector. From 2014 to 2022, he served first as deputy chair, then as chief executive officer, of the Singapore Symphony Group; under his leadership, the Singapore Symphony Orchestra was awarded third place in Gramophone magazine’s Orchestra of the Year 2021, the only Asian orchestra among the nominees. Prior, he spent a decade at the management consultancy Bain & Company. He currently serves on the boards of Library and Archives Solutions, a subsidiary of Singapore’s National Library Board, and Duke-NUS Medical School, and chairs the advisory council of Chua Chu Kang Secondary School. Chng is a PhD candidate in history at the National University of Singapore as well as a long-time volunteer docent for local institutions such as the Asian Civilizations Museum.

In a press release, Chng described the appointment as an opportunity to continue “making the arts accessible and meaningful to our communities . . . [and] to strengthen the role that the arts play in our society.” NGS chairman Peter Ho welcomed the appointment, stating that Chng’s “record of transforming the beloved ensembles of the Singapore Symphony Group speaks for itself,” and that they are “confident the Gallery is in good hands as it continues to grow its voice for Singapore and Southeast Asian art.”

Tan has held the role of NGS director since 2013 and took on the directorship of SAM in 2019. He was appointed CEO of both institutions in 2024. In stepping back from the NGS, Tan said he was “grateful to have had the privilege of leading both NGS and SAM,” and that this is “the right time for each to benefit from dedicated leadership.”

The joint statement framed the split as reflecting “the continued development of both institutions as they enter a new phase of growth,” while noting the two museums will remain “natural partners” that continue to work closely in promoting and showcasing art and culture from Singapore and beyond.

Harison Butler is an editorial intern at ArtAsiaPacific.
excerpt_original: Chng succeeds Eugene Tan, who will focus his leadership at the Singapore Art Museum. Harison Butler

article_text:
Earlier this month, the Trylon in Minneapolis gave audiences six chances over three days to see “Kanał,” Andrzej Wajda’s 1957 film about Polish resistance fighters retreating into the sewers of Warsaw. After opening night, programmer John Moret saw enthusiastic reviews on Letterboxd .

The next evening, he says, ticket sales picked up.

Moret could imagine the calculation for somebody still on the fence: “Oh, these people I trust went to go see this movie, and they loved it. And it’s just playing for two more days.”

On November 5, the New York Times reported that its parent company was in exclusive talks to buy Letterboxd for roughly $330 million. Under the deal being discussed, the popular film-logging site would likely keep operating on its own but use the Times Company’s advertising technology.

For theaters like the Trylon, what matters is whether cinephiles who went on opening night can still reach those who might go tomorrow. In 2026, that handoff is working remarkably well on Letterboxd.

Five days before “Kanał” opened, Ken Russell’s “The Devils” sold out at the Trylon on election night . Moret also co-founded the national Programmers’ Jam with Bret Berg, theatrical sales director at the American Genre Film Archive, and Dan Halsted of Portland’s Hollywood Theatre. When the Jam met in Los Angeles in May, Berg told IndieWire that programmers had access to more restorations than ever before; plus, more places to show them and a new audience coming through the doors.

We helped declare it the Golden Age of Repertory programming this spring. And when we spoke with Berg again this month, he said Letterboxd still drives “the FOMO of needing to be conversant in a movie of the moment.” For at least a few days in Minneapolis, that movie was “Kanał.”

Berg can see why a press company might be a good home for Letterboxd. He also remembers what the last sale made plain to him: Something cinephiles had spent years building was ultimately “just an asset to be bought and sold.” In the r/Letterboxd thread about the talks , one commenter saw an upside to a newspaper owning a site that rates movies. They also worried about paywalled features and ads, but liked the prospect of a ratings system free of “studios putting their fingers on the scale.”

How Moviegoers and Programmers Use Letterboxd Differently

If you come home from seeing a rep movie and write what you thought about it, your friends get a recommendation, the theater gets a little local press, Letterboxd itself gets something to put an ad next to, and as a matter of historical record? Years later, a “Kanał” fan who’s never even been to Minneapolis can land on the same page and read what it was like to see it with your crowd.

That’s a powerful engine for word-of-mouth, particularly among the very online. Moret keeps his own movie diary in a paper notebook these days, and told us he actually stopped posting what he watched on Letterboxd for a while because Trylon customers kept asking if that meant he was going to program it. “Sometimes a guy just wants to watch a movie,” he said.

Moret still regularly checks Letterboxd after screenings and uses that data to help shape his local scene. “I can see that night exactly how they responded,” he said. Moret said he’s seen Trylon patrons meet theater volunteers and follow them on Letterboxd afterward. He’s also heard from people who knew one another by their Letterboxd handles before they started going to showings together. Their community has real taste, and Moret’s job is to help subtly steer that momentum in exciting artistic directions.

He did have an ulterior motive for December’s Dede Allen series .

Moret explained to IndieWire that he wanted to show “Mike’s Murder,” James Bridges’ 1984 mystery starring Debra Winger as a bank teller trying to find out who killed her tennis instructor, and realized a Letterboxd user could make a pretty good list out of movies you didn’t know shared an editor like Allen. So, he put multiple of the craftsman’s offerings on the calendar — effectively allowing Trylon visitors to use a popular classic like “Dog Day Afternoon” on December 11 as an avenue toward “Mike’s Murder” on December 18. (Of course, both play in 35mm.)

On the supply end at the American Genre Film Archive, Berg reads the reviews from one town with the next town in mind. A joke review with thousands of likes might tell him very little about who’d pay to see a movie. But five people leaving a one-off screening at a DIY microcinema and feeling compelled to write about it could tell him quite a lot.

For someone deciding which films in the archive’s catalog deserve another look, that’s “some interesting free data,” and even Berg comes across movies he’s never heard of. Three and a half stars on Letterboxd is enough to make him give one a closer look. Then, he wants to know what kind of time people had. “How many audience moments are there? That’s what I care about.”

For a horror movie, he might be counting jump scares. With Herzog, he’s thinking about how many iconic images there are. (Referencing Les Blank’s “Ship of Dreams,” I personally suggested that the nation craves the sight of a steamship being pushed up a mountain. “Oh, it’s true,” Berg said.)

Berg also named Spectacle in Brooklyn and Whammy! in Los Angeles as places where he could count on hearing from a few people whether a movie made an impression. He said he can look for the same things he would on any research viewing, but with the added benefit of a crowd that makes a significant difference. Was everybody there to see a new restoration? How full was the room exactly?

Berg could always pick up the phone and ask someone like Moret how a screening went in Minneapolis. But Letterboxd gives them both a way to see and respond to the same information, connecting what happens in one theater to what programmers are noticing hit elsewhere.

Berg also thinks about who’s had the chance to write film books previously, and who has been taken seriously as a critic on a national stage. He singled out trans critics among the writers who can find an audience on Letterboxd without first persuading an editor to commission a review. In the end, the person who finally gets you to watch a movie might write three sentences half a century after the original reviews ran. They might also be the only person you encounter who’s heard of it.

Do Your Followers Follow You?

If the people writing those Letterboxd reviews scatter across half a dozen sites, Berg could still go looking for them but it would take longer. And if Letterboxd imploded altogether, he’d expect “a return to gut feeling” that wouldn’t be bad — but might give the audience less of a voice.

Berg has some experience with the decision to leave. He still uses Vimeo for his day job, but the price helped persuade him to move his own project, Museum of Home Video , to a cheaper service. Finding another place to stream was manageable, and the Letterboxd equivalent of that transition is doable for most users too. First, it would mean finding another place to put your film log and reviews. Then, you’d have to find the people whose retro picks and ideas got you to sign up in the first place.

In that same Letterboxd Reddit thread, one person was already looking for the exit. “Any other apps people know about with similar list-building functionality?” they asked.

Andrew Masyk, the founder of rival tracking site Simkl, says its importer can bring over your watchlist, ratings, and the full text of your reviews, and custom lists can come over using a separate tool. That said, the comments and follows stay behind. “People have to find each other again, and that’s the hardest part of moving,” he wrote.

Masyk has every business reason to make switching easy. Even so, he figures people who have spent years keeping a movie diary on Letterboxd are mostly inclined to stay put. “What moves people is the product changing under them: core features going behind a paywall, heavier ads, or getting your data out becoming harder.” His test for a buyer is whether they keep that exit open. “The export button matters more than who owns the company,” he wrote.

Yes, the export button can save a Letterboxd review but the friend who used to see it in their feed still has to find it — and that can get more difficult long before anyone actually leaves Letterboxd. If a buyer gave sponsored posts more room in the feed, for instance, you could still log every film you see while missing the three sentences from a friend that would’ve gotten you to your local theater in time.

If Letterboxd breaks, the Trylon loses one way to fill a seat, and a programmer in another town loses one way to tell whether “Kanał” might fill a few seats there, too. As for regular film fans? Hear about “Kanał” on Monday, and you can go. Hear about it on Wednesday, and you’ve missed the boat.
excerpt_original: Repertory theaters have been a bright spot in a rough stretch for Hollywood. A possible Letterboxd sale raises concerns about how old movies find new audiences — and what happens if those young cinephiles scatter.
image_alt: What Happens If We Break Letterboxd?

title_original: How Did ‘American Gothic’ Become So Iconic? This Art Historian Spent Five Decades Investigating.
editorial_title_zh: 《美国哥特式》是如何成为如此标志性的作品的？这位艺术史学家花了五十年时间进行研究。

Ellison）这样的艺术家来说，复制一对夫妇摆姿势站在家族住宅前的母题，成了讲述移民故事的一种方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "科恩对《美国哥特式》受欢迎程度的解释是，它展示了婚姻的原型——这一母题可以从古埃及王子追溯到伊特鲁里亚的 terracotta 陶器再到荷兰黄金时代肖像画——并以一种适合现代时代的易懂方式呈现出来。然而，与其他那些例子不同的是，在伍德画作光滑的表面之下，隐藏着一种莫名的不安，这种张力赋予了画作生机，并推动了对它的改编。可能为同性恋的伍德在画完《美国哥特式》五年后经历了自己失败的婚姻。如果说他的美学体现的是直言不讳的价值观，那么他也具备独特的能力，能够捕捉到当现实与形式的期望相碰撞时——正如经常发生的那样——所有那些无法言说的东西。", article_text:
In need of a couple’s costume this Halloween? Try a calico apron over a dark dress, a low bun with one loose strand, a cameo broach at your throat; dress a partner in overalls and wire-rimmed glasses, holding a three-pronged pitchfork. It won’t take much to be immediately recognizable as the duo from American Gothic , Grant Wood’s 1930 painting and subject of Wanda Corn’s new book, The Couple with the Pitchfork: American Gothic from Easel to Icon. Why, Corn wants to know, did this painting become so iconic?

Corn, an eminent scholar of American art, has been thinking about this question for five decades. The painting intersected with her own trajectory as an art historian and with her personal history as a descendent of the Midwest: the book includes a photograph of her grandparents posed side-by-side at their home in Indiana, her grandfather in denim overalls, and her grandmother with hair pulled back and a homemade dress. The parallels between the family photograph and American Gothic show how thoroughly Wood, himself raised in Iowa, was tapping in to regional Midwestern identity. Yet a portrait of a midwestern couple is hardly a promising candidate for global fame.

Of course, the pair in American Gothic aren’t a couple, at least not in Wood’s view. He claimed to have intended the twosome to represent a small-town father and daughter, basing the figures on his sister Nan and his dentist. When he made the painting, Wood was searching for a way of working that would be distinctive to the Midwest. He’d tried his hand at French Impressionism, taking several trips to Paris, and worked as a decorator back home in Cedar Rapids. Growing support for the arts in small town America, funded by philanthropists including the Carnegie Foundation, created more opportunities for Wood to make work that felt characteristic of his region.

American Gothic marked Wood’s embrace of a new style as an Iowa painter, developing a pictorial language suited to the visual culture of the Midwest. Rather than straightforward realism, Corn shows American Gothic to be the product of a thorough engagement with pattern and form. Vertical lines, from the tines of the pitchfork to the church steeple in the background, organize and order the composition. Round and oval forms—the figures’ long faces, the woman’s brooch, the pattern on the calico, the shape of the man’s ears—create harmony within the scene. Wood identified what he called a “decorative” quality in his subject matter, basic geometries and hard lines that he translated into paint with such precision that the work was taken to be self-evident rather than deeply thought.

The painting was immediately misunderstood. After winning a prize in a juried exhibition at the Art Institute of Chicago, American Gothic —which reproduced well in newsprint thanks to those straightforward, geometric forms—became a sensation. Labeled by the press as a farmer and his wife, the depiction of the couple found detractors in both Iowans and art critics. Locals saw the pitchfork as outdated—four tines would have been more appropriate—and the woman unforgivably dour. Critics couldn’t place the work, finding it out of step with modernist abstraction. Everyone agreed it was an image of marriage.

For Corn, this misunderstanding is key to the painting’s success, allowing for endless adaptation of the archetypal form of two figures joined in union. She traces the painting’s influence in both art and popular culture, drawing on a personal archive of hundreds of reappropriations of the work: American Gothics in butter at a state fair, gay American Gothics in support of same-sex marriage, feminist American Gothics showing the woman heading off to work. Surprisingly, for a painting often dismissed as conservative and reactionary, some of the first adopters of its form were Black urban artists who saw the painting in Chicago in the 1930s. (The Art Institute acquired the painting soon after it debuted.) Certain African American artists saw in Wood a model for a self-taught artist from farm country. Reproducing the motif of a couple posed before a family home became a way of telling stories about migration for artists like Walter Ellison.

Corn’s explanation for American Gothic’s popularity is that it shows the archetype of marriage, a motif that can be traced from Egyptian princes to Etruscan terra cottas to Dutch golden age portraits, rendered in an accessible manner for the modern era. Yet unlike those other examples, beneath the smooth surface of Wood’s painting is a felt unease, a tension that animates the painting and motivates its adaptation. Wood, likely gay, experienced his own failed marriage five years after painting American Gothic. If his aesthetic was one of plainspoken values, he was also singularly able to capture all that goes unsaid when, as is so often the case, reality strains against the expectations of form.
excerpt_original: A portrait of a midwestern couple is hardly a promising candidate for global fame.

article_text:
田中久貴による写真展「大廈 The Buildings, Mansions.」が、2026年10月13日から18日まで大阪・心斎橋のギャラリー・ソラリスで開催される。

タイトルの「大廈」とは、中国語でビルや大きな建物を意味する言葉。本作で田中が向き合ったのは、2025年8月の香港だ。地下鉄やトラムを乗り継ぎ、高温多湿の街を歩きながら、建て増しと積層を繰り返す高層住宅や、その窓から突き出すエアコンの室外機、ベランダのない窓辺に干された洗濯物など、都市に刻まれた日常の光景を撮影した。かつて香港のイメージを形づくっていた無数のネオンサインは減少し、九龍寨城は公園となり、啓徳空港もすでに閉鎖されている。田中がカメラを向けるのは、そうした過去の香港へのノスタルジーというより、変貌を続ける都市の現在だ。隙間なく林立する巨大な集合住宅を見上げながら、そのスケールとは裏腹に感じられる「せせこましさ」や、建築の表面から漏れ出す生活の痕跡をモノクロームの画面へと取り込んでいく。

田中はステートメントで、大廈から「冷徹な眼で凝視」される感覚について記している。都市を一方的に観察するのではなく、自らもまた都市から見返される存在として身を置き、そこへ飛び込んでくる「日常としての香港」を受け入れる。その視線の往復から、建築物そのものだけでなく、そこに暮らす人々の存在や時間が浮かび上がる。

本作は2026年、文芸社「写真集大賞」で最優秀賞を受賞。同名写真集『大廈』として9月15日に刊行された。本展では写真集に収められた作品から16点を展示する。

タイトル

田中久貴 写真展「大廈 The Buildings, Mansions.」

場所

ギャラリー・ソラリス（大阪府大阪市中央区南船場3-2-6 大阪農林会館B1F）

会期

2026年10月13日（火）〜18日（日）

時間

12:00〜19:00（最終日18:00まで）

休み

無し

料金

無料

URL

https://solaris-g.com/portfolio_page/261013/

article_translation_json: [{"type": "image", "url": "https://imaonline.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tanaka2.jpg", "alt": "塔纳卡2", "caption": "", "credit": "IMA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "田中久貴的照片展「大厦 The Buildings, Mansions.」將於2026年10月13日至18日在大阪心薩橋的畫廊索拉里斯舉行。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "标题的“大楼”是中国语中的意思建筑和大建筑的词,本作中田中遇到了2025年8月的香港,通过地铁和电车,沿着高温和潮湿的城市行走,重复建造和积层的高层住宅,从窗户出发的空调的室外飞机,无缝窗口干燥的洗衣物等,拍摄了城市的日常景色。曾经塑造香港形象的无数内昂信号减少,九龙齐城成为公园,啓徳机场也已经关闭,田中将相机转向的是那些过去的香港的诺斯塔尔吉,而不是不断变化的城市的现在。看着无间断地森林的巨型集合住宅,与其规模背后感受到的“<unk>”或从建筑的表面泄漏的生命的痕迹,将其插入到单克罗姆的屏幕上。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "田中在一份声明中写道,从大楼“冷细眼观察”的感觉,而不是单方面观察城市,而是自己也把自己作为从城市回顾的存在,接受到那里跳跃的“日常香港”。从眼光的旅行,不仅建筑本身,而且居住在那里的人的存在和时间浮现。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这部作品于2026年在文艺术社“照片集大奖”中获最佳奖,并于9月15日作为同名照片集“大楼”出版,展览将展示16点从照片集中收集的作品。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "标题", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "田中久貴 照片展「大建築物, Mansions」", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "地点", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "画廊 索拉里斯(大阪府大阪市中央区南船场3-2-6 大阪農林會館B1F)", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "會議期", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "2026年10月13日(火)至18日(日)", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "时间", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "12:00 至 19:00 (最后一天至 18:00 )", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "假期", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "没有", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "费用", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "免费", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "URL", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "https://solaris-g.com/portfolio_page/261013/", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "为了防止新型科罗纳病毒传播,我们网站上发布的展览和活动内容可能会发生变化,请在官方网站上查看最新信息等。", "translated": true}]

Haines）和索拉布·诺希尔瓦尼（Sohrab Noshirvani）（代表作《毛里塔尼亚人》、《告密者》）将担任该片编剧。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "常驻柏林的导演阿米尔·法赫尔·埃尔丁出生于乌克兰基辅，父母来自戈兰高地，是叙利亚人。他表示：“Caesar的故事承载着巨大的责任。在宏大事件的背后，是一个个体面临非凡抉择时深具人性色彩的故事，以及在后果几乎不可想象时采取行动所需要的勇气。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该项目最初由卡塔尔电影委员会（Qatar Film Committee）在2025年首届多哈产业日期间宣布。该委员会是卡塔尔媒体城（Media City Qatar）枢纽下的官方机构，旨在推动该国娱乐产业的发展。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "卡塔尔电影委员会主席、卡塔尔律师哈桑·阿尔-萨瓦迪（Hassan Al Thawadi）评论道：“Caesar的故事是一个关于非凡勇气、牺牲和全球影响的故事。当我们去年宣布这个项目时，我们的雄心是组建一个能够以应有的人文关怀、敏感度和电影雄心来呈现他故事的演员与创意团队。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "拉罗卡在记者会上指出，“像这样性质的电影能够获得我们所得到的这种资源和支持水平，是非常罕见的。”他感谢了阿尔-萨瓦迪及其他合作伙伴，“感谢他们为我们提供了必要的支持，使我们能够努力制作出符合国际最高水准的电影。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我希望我们明年能回到这里，宣布重要的制作里程碑，”他说道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "多哈电影节第二届于11月19日至27日在卡塔尔首都举行。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Ameer Fakher Eldin (“The Stranger,” “Yunan”) is set to direct Neon-backed biopic “Caesar.” The film centers on Syrian military officer Farid Al-Madhhan who blew the whistle on torture and killings perpetrated by the regime of Syrian president Bashar Assad.

Syrian star Taim Hassan has been cast in the lead role playing the film’s titular hero, who’s nom de guerre was Caesar. Farid Al-Madhhan was a military police photographer and head of the judicial evidence office in Damascus.

Related Stories

‘Home Alone’ Reboot in the Works at Disney from Macaulay Culkin, Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg

Adam Driver Explains Why He's Starring in Marvel's 'X-Men' Reboot After Years of Turning Down MCU Offers: 'Felt Like the Right Time'

Al-Madhhan launched a secret operation to smuggle more than 50,000 photographs out of Syria showing evidence of torture, starvation and murder in the country’s lockups. This evidence marked a turning point in Syrian history, prompting European prosecutors to take legal proceeding against the Assad government’s war crimes.

The dictator’s reign of terror ended in December 2024 after a 13-year civil war that caused more than 500,000 deaths and forced millions of Syrians to leave their homeland.

Hassan has played the lead in hit Arabic TV show “Al Hayba,” about a family of arms smugglers working the border between Syria and Lebanon, a role that made him a household name across the region and reached international audiences on Netflix. His more recent work includes the show “Taj” (2024), in which he plays a boxer resisting the French occupation of Syria; hit political drama “Under the Seventh Ground” (2025); and thriller series “Mawlana” (2026).

The high-end biopic was unveiled during an emotionally charged press conference held during the Industry Days of the Doha Film Festival , attended by a broad panel. The panel included both Taim Hassan, set to play Caesar, and the real Farid Al-Madhhan. (They are pictured above, from left to right) .

Al-Madhhan pointed out that the upcoming film about his act – which carried extreme danger of torture and murder by Syrian authorities – will not be “a forensic or documentary exercise.”

“It is a human story – the story of people who had lives, families and experiences, but whose lives unfortunately ended in inhumane circumstances. That is why we decided to tell this story through cinema: to give a voice to the human beings who suffered,” he said.

“Seeing the actor and the person he is portraying sitting together is quite remarkable,” noted U.S. producer Mike Larocca, co-founder of Department M. “It is like looking in a mirror,” he added. “I think we have managed to find the right actor.”

The “Caesar” project is being developed by Department M and Doha’s Katara Studios, with distribution in place via Neon and support from Kuwait-based studio Sard Media. Syrian production company Tadmor Film City is also on board.

BAFTA-nominated screenwriting duo Rory Haines and Sohrab Noshirvani (“The Mauritanian,” “Informer”) are on board to write the screenplay.

Berlin-based helmer Ameer Fakher Eldin, who was born in Kyiv, Ukraine, to Syrian parents from the Golan Heights, said: “Caesar’s story carries enormous responsibility. Behind the scale of the events is the deeply human story of an individual confronted with an extraordinary choice, and the courage required to act when the consequences were almost unimaginable.”

The project had been first announced during the first edition of the Doha Industry Days in 2025 by the Qatar Film Committee, an official body that is part of the Media City Qatar hub tasked with driving growth of the country’s entertainment industry.

Commented Hassan Al Thawadi, the Qatari lawyer who chairs the Qatar Film Committee: “Caesar’s story is one of extraordinary courage, sacrifice and global consequence. When we announced this project last year, our ambition was to assemble a cast and creative team capable of approaching his story with the humanity, sensitivity and cinematic ambition it deserves.”

Larocca at the press conference noted that “it is very rare for a film of this nature to receive the level of resources and support that we have received.” He thanked Al Thawadi and the other partners “for giving us the support necessary to attempt to make a film of the highest possible quality by international standards.”

“I hope we will be back here next year to announce significant production milestones,” he said.

The Doha Film Festival’s second edition runs Nov. 19-27 in the Qatari capital.

article_text:
[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published on April 24, 2026, when “ I Swear ” was released in American theaters. Aramayo recently won Best Actor in a Film at the BAFTA Scotland Awards . The film and his performance are eligible for this year’s Oscars, and “I Swear” is now streaming on Netflix.]

When Robert Aramayo signed on to play Scottish Tourette’s activist John Davidson in filmmaker Kirk Jones’ biopic “I Swear,” he could scarcely imagine where the film would take him.

A hit in the UK, the film netted Aramayo a pair of BAFTA wins earlier in the year , as the British actor won both the vaunted Rising Star Award (previous winners include James McAvoy, John Boyega, Tom Holland, Tom Hardy, and those are just some of its biggest names) and the Best Actor trophy (beating out Timothée Chalamet, Leonardo DiCaprio, Ethan Hawke, Jesse Plemons, and eventual Oscar winner Michael B. Jordan).

But that’s hardly all that happened at the February awards show , which was instantly and forever marred by a number of loud, racist outbursts from Davidson himself that were directed at “Sinners” stars Jordan, Delroy Lindo, Wunmi Mosaku , and more. The fallout from the incident was both swift and prolonged, and will likely impact the domestic release of “I Swear,” which is rolling out in stateside theaters now.

Aramayo’s performance in the film is indeed star-making and awards-worthy, as he brings sensitivity and great courage to his portrayal of Davidson, following him from his earliest symptoms through his current passionate activism. Hopefully, viewers can see and appreciate the work on its own merits, and get to know Aramayo much better, though he has previously appeared in plenty of projects recognizable to American audiences, from “The Empty Man” to “The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” to a little thing called “Game of Thrones” (young Ned Stark!).

Ahead, Aramayo tells IndieWire about his deep research for the role, everything BAFTAs, and what he hopes will come from more people seeing the film and, hopefully, understanding Tourette’s all the better.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: When I saw the film at TIFF in September , I did my due diligence before I reviewed it, and learned that John is a huge figure in the UK, but relatively unknown in America. How much did you know about him before this film?

Robert Aramayo: John’s made a lot of documentaries, but the big one that probably had the most impact was “John’s Not Mad,” and that was in 1989. So if you speak to people who were around then, they have a lot of very personal stories about watching that documentary and being like, “Wow, is this Tourette’s? What’s Tourette’s?”

So when you get the script, are you someone who then wants to do more research into him, or do you feel like the script is the thing?

The production team and Kirk were so gracious, and they gave me so much time. I think they were like, “Oh, yeah, take a couple of months or something to research and stuff.” I was really thankful for that. The first thing that I did was to meet John; I met him very quickly. And then I went away for a month, and I spent that time gaining as much knowledge as I could about Tourette’s and what it is. That was through watching the documentaries, watching YouTube videos, and reading books.

I based myself in Galashiels and spent weeks with John, just following him around and spending as much time with him as I could. And also traveling through Scotland, meeting people, mainly through [support organization] Tourette Scotland, who lived with Tourette’s as well. I wanted to have, I don’t know, a more expansive view of Tourette’s than just John. Obviously, John was my main focus, though.

When you’re getting ready to meet John, what were you expecting and anticipating? What were you nervous about?

I don’t know what I felt, really. I was so filled with anxiety about, oh my word, am I going to do this? I wanted John to like me. I was already feeling, God, this is going to be a really big challenge. And I met him within days of saying yes.

But then, when I met him, one thing that struck me straight away was his knowledge. He’s got a really amazing knowledge about, obviously, Tourette’s, but also a lot of neurodiversity and how it lives, other conditions that exist with Tourette’s, and stuff like that. He’s got a lot of thoughts about how we can do better and help young people and things like that. He’s very forthcoming with it.

He’s got so much heart. He’s such an amazing, welcoming, supportive man that I was just like, wow, this is a really impressive person that I’m meeting here. Of course, then your anxiety and the responsibility meter have gone through the roof.

Just watching the film, I learned so much about what Tourette’s can entail and the very wide spectrum of symptoms that people can have. What was the most unexpected thing you learned about it during your research?

A couple of things really that had a really big impact on me straight away, and that sort of broke my perception of what I thought Tourette’s was, that anything can be a tic, and that it’s so singular to the person. So if you’ve met one person with Tourette’s, someone said to me, you’ve met one person with Tourette’s . That was a big thing.

And also the fact that there’s a lot of tics that you just don’t see. There’s tics that you don’t see as tics because anything can be a tic, or there’s tics that exist only in somebody’s mind, and things like that, tics linked with OCD. Just the complexity of it was massive.

I learned some statistics recently, which I found really interesting: One in 50 kids in America live with persistent tic disorder, and one in 160 live with Tourette’s , so it’s unbelievably common, it’s everywhere. We have met people with Tourette’s, we meet them all the time. It was part of the experience of the film as well, we met loads of people who were living with Tourette’s undiagnosed. 50 percent of people who live with Tourette’s in the U.S. are undiagnosed, and that was true for us in the UK as well in our experience. Maybe the thing is that we don’t know that that’s what’s happening. That made me think, wow, there’s a real educational piece to this as well.

You are playing someone who is a real person who has been captured on film for many years. People know what he looks like, they know what he sounds like. How do you find the line between impersonation and impression in your performance?

I never wanted to impersonate John. I think I would’ve gone the wrong way if that was what I was thinking. You have to, at a certain point, take ownership of the character and try and make him your own. I was lucky because there was so much that I needed to learn, so for so long, I wasn’t thinking about performance or playing him at all. I was just trying to immerse myself as much as I could in everything, anything that I could get my hands on. Then, at certain point, I moved to thinking about how I was going to try and play my version of John.

In a [narrative] film, you get the opportunity to maybe show a little bit more [than a documentary]. A documentary film crew comes into somebody’s life and they can capture what they can capture, but we could capture way more intimate moments throughout the whole film that John had spoken to.

We could show the moments where he is on his own, whether there’s been an impact or how he’s feeling or his emotional life, how things change over time and stuff like that, and hopefully try and do it with truth and authenticity.

You attended Juilliard, which always seems a little, “Oooohhh, he’s Juilliard -trained.”

[Laughs]

But now that you’re a few years out of school, what are the pieces of training that are proving to be most useful to you?

I think that acting teachers and drama school is vocabulary, really. At the time, certain things that teachers would say to me had a massive impact on me and really opened me up to other ways of looking at things, and other things are only impacting me now, as I keep working and as I get older. I think that’s the beauty of drama school, you get flooded with all of this stuff, and then you’re going, “Oh, that’s what they were talking about.” And then there’s things that my teachers would consistently say, “You’ve got to work on this, you’ve got to work on this,” and I’m still working on it. It’s like a toolbox, and every now and again you go, “Oh, yeah, that’s what I need.”

They also made us do liberal arts which — I’m from Yorkshire, I don’t even know what liberal arts meant — but I’d encounter Nietzsche and Plato and all this stuff. I had no time at all to digest anything, but I’d read it and be like, “I don’t really know what’s going on here, but I think this is going to be important one day. I think I’m going to reread this one day!”

What was the morning of the BAFTA nominations like for you?

I knew it was happening that morning. I remember talking to my agent, and we just didn’t speak about it, but we both knew that they were coming out that morning or whatever, so we had a really chill conversation about something else. [Laughs] I put it on in the background, because I thought we had a chance at, I don’t know, something , and then I heard that Peter had been nominated and I was so happy for him. I was elated for him.

So, I was just in that, and I was doing the dishes, and I was like, “Wow, that’s so cool. I can’t wait to go text him.” And then they said my name, and I just absolutely couldn’t believe it. My agent called me back straight away and was like, “Oh, my God.” It was an amazing feeling, but it was really unexpected because I was still really, really sort of overwhelmed by the Rising Star thing.

You genuinely looked so surprised when you won Best Actor at the show. I feel like I would black out in that moment. Do you remember what that moment felt like?

Yeah, because I almost did! I had this weird physical reaction where I sort of went back [ pantomimes sitting way back ], and I think somebody grabbed me. I think I would’ve just kept going. I would’ve fallen off my chair or something.

I honestly couldn’t believe it. I’m honestly not sure I still can believe that that’s something that happened to me, because for someone like me to be in that group of people blew my mind. I felt like, “Wow, and there I am, that’s my name.” To me, that was the thing that sort of really, really, really, really blew me away. When it happened, yes, it all just becomes a blur, and I’m running down the stairs, and I don’t know what the hell I’m going to say.

Obviously, other things happened at the awards show involving John. As someone who had seen the film, I felt like I had a greater grasp on what was happening; I had that context. Now that the film is coming out in America, what hopes do you have for people seeing the film and how that might impact that conversation?

I think lots of people watch the film, and they feel like their education around Tourette’s has improved and increased, and that would be amazing [if that continued]. I think it’s important to acknowledge that … Tourette’s has an impact on a person who’s ticcing, and the same tic obviously has an impact on the person who’s receiving the tic or impacted by the tic. And it’s important to acknowledge that, because that is what it is. Coprolalia, which is the tic that John has, that tic, it’s not saying what you think , it’s saying the worst thing imaginable . That’s how it was described to me.

I hope people watch the film. And I hope people watch the film and think, “Oh, I’ve learned something about Tourette’s.” I hope that people watch the film from the community, because that’s been an amazing thing as well. People watching it who have lived with Tourette’s or lived with another neurodiverse condition have reached out and said, “I see myself in this.” You want people to go to the movies and enjoy the film, but if people go home and Google “John Davidson” or Google “Tourette’s,” that’d be amazing.

The film is going to introduce you to a much larger audience, but you’ve also been in some massive hits before this one. Which is a fun way to ask: Do you know that “The Empty Man” has a huge cult fandom?

[Laughs] I’ve been told this. What an experience. I loved making that film. It was a long journey with it, and I learned a lot. And it was my first movie that I’d done with James Badge Dale, and I did another one with him as well. And I really, really liked working with him. He’s a really nice guy, and he’s a really talented actor. And the director, David [Prior], was wonderful. I learned a lot on that film. I love that people love that film.

You are also in the “Lord of the Rings” world as well. Are you going to be turning out to see “The Hunt for Gollum”?

I’m so excited. I can’t wait. I’m a massive fan of the Peter Jackson films. I can’t wait to see what they do with it. It’s a really interesting story. I’m glad that they’re doing it and doing it properly.

Now that you’ve had what feels like a big breakthrough, what sort of things are you pursuing next?

What do I want to do next? I don’t know! I feel lucky to just be an actor, to work. I’ve been lucky enough to work with some incredible people on “I Swear,” to work with Kirk and Peter and Shirley and Maxine. People like that, you learn, you grow, you get better. And so if I can just keep doing it, I’ll be happy.

That Rising Star Award feels like a lot of pressure!

I just feel really, really grateful for everyone who voted for me. It’s such a cool award that the public, the British public , vote for you. I feel so grateful for everyone who voted for me. I just feel very, very grateful for the whole thing, for everything, and mainly that people hopefully watch the film and talk about it.

For more information about Tourette Syndrome and access to free resources and support, visit the Tourette Association of America right here .
excerpt_original: The "I Swear" star nabbed two BAFTAs at this year's fraught ceremony, but as he tells IndieWire, the next step isn't more glory — it's just more audience members, more knowledge, and hopefully more understanding.

article_text:
Proyectos Monclova Gallery (Booth #D38) announces its debut presentation at Paris Photo , on view at the Grand Palais , with a solo booth devoted to Hungarian-born Mexican photographer Kati Horna (1912 – 2000). This follows the gallery’s recent announcement of exclusive representation of the Estate of Kati Horna and marks the first time the gallery has dedicated its participation in an international photography fair to the work of a single artist. A retrospective of Kati Horna, curated by Daniel Garza Usabiaga, is now on view at the Museo del Palacio de Bellas Artes in Mexico City through February 7, 2027.

Born in Szilasbalhás, Hungary, Horna settled in Mexico after the outbreak of the Second World War. She resided in Mexico until her death, producing a fundamental part of her work there. The presentation traces various stages of Horna’s career—from her years in Paris in the 1930s to her portraits of artists made in Mexico and her collaborations with the magazine S.nob in the 1960s—and reveals how she developed the modernist eye that earned her a significant place in avant-garde photography.

Horna arrived in Paris in 1933 and during her early years in the city would produce the series Marchés aux puces (Flea Markets) and Cafés de París (Paris Cafés) , works from which will be on view at the booth. Flea markets also drew other foreign photographers working in the city, such as André Kertész, Brassaï and Germaine Krull; in the streets and cafés of Paris, Horna captured everyday life and the city’s spaces of leisure, with a singular ability to find humor and intimacy in the ordinary.

The booth will also reflect a selection of works developed in Mexico City, following Horna’s move there in 1939. In Mexico City, Horna and her husband, the Spanish artist José Horna, became part of a community of exiled European artists and intellectuals. Portraits of two central figures of that circle, the English painter Leonora Carrington and the Spanish artist Remedios Varo, with whom Horna shared close personal and creative bonds, will figure on the booth.

Also featured are two series made for the “Fetiches” section of S.nob , the magazine founded by Salvador Elizondo, Juan García Ponce and Emilio García Riera. Oda a la necrofilia (Ode to Necrophilia) , published in the first issue, was conceived as a staged scene in collaboration with Leonora Carrington: a woman dressed in black, her face hidden beneath a veil, embodies death. In Paraísos artificiales (Artificial Paradises) , for which cultural promoter Luz del Amo posed, the uncanny emerges from the meeting of the living and the inanimate, the sinister and the familiar.

Further emphasizing Horna’s collaborations with Leonora Carrington will be works from the series Mujer y máscara (Woman and Mask) . Mujer y máscara was made for Mexico This Month , the magazine edited by Anita Brenner to which Horna contributed between 1958 and 1965. The mask that appears in Horna’s images was made by Leonora Carrington.

With this selection, Proyectos Monclova Gallery highlights Kati Horna’s significance for the history of photography in Mexico and for the country’s artistic avant-gardes through a practice that moved between documentary, portraiture, experimentation and staged photography.

About Kati Horna

Kati Horna (b. Szilasbalhás (now Mezőszilas), Hungary, 1912, d. Mexico City, 2000) was a Hungarian-born avant-garde photographer and a seminal figure in twentieth-century photography in Mexico. Her career unfolded across Hungary, Germany, France, Spain, and, above all, Mexico, where she settled and lived for much of her life. Her photographic practice encompassed a wide range of genres, including war photojournalism, documentary and street photography, portraiture, and architectural photography—reflecting both her political convictions and her interest in the encounter between the everyday and the fantastic. She also developed avant-garde artistic approaches through experimentation with photographic materials, the use of photomontage, and a visual language associated with Surrealism. She is considered one of the most important figures of the Surrealist Photography movement in the country, alongside Leonora Carrington and Remedios Varo.

Her work in Mexico coincided with the beginning of a long period of economic expansion and urban growth in the country, and she quickly became involved with the graphic press in Mexico City, with which she collaborated until the end of her career. Among the numerous Mexican publications for which she worked were Nosotros, Tiempo, Mujeres: Expresión femenina, Revista de la Universidad de México, Arquitectura México, Mexico This Month, and Diseño. Her photographic production reveals the rapid transformation of the city and its vibrant cultural life in the mid-twentieth century.

About Proyectos Monclova

Established in 2005, Proyectos Monclova is a leading contemporary art gallery based in Mexico City. The gallery represents a roster of some of Mexico’s most acclaimed contemporary artists, including young and mid-career artists, alongside established great masters. In 2010, the gallery sought to bolster its programming by bringing in international artists, further enriching its dialogue.

Proyectos Monclova has become a vital force within the Mexican art world, playing a critical role in expanding Mexico’s presence on the global art scene and participating in numerous prestigious international art fairs. The gallery continues to advance its mission by offering a dynamic program that enriches both local and international discourse through notable exhibitions, institutional collaborations, artist initiatives, and scholarly publications.

Man kann sagen, dass Filme immer politisch sind, allein schon durch die Kameraposition, wie Jean-Luc Godard das gesagt hat. Ich bin gegen vieles, was gerade passiert, nicht nur gegen den Krieg in Gaza oder in der Ukraine, sondern auch gegen das, was ICE in den Vereinigten Staaten anstellt, oder was in Mexiko geschieht, wo so viele Menschen verschwinden und zahllose Femizide passieren. Die Liste ist sehr lang. Wie sich diese Themen aber in Filmen wiederfinden, hängt von den einzelnen Filmemachern und Filmemacherinnen ab.", "links": [{"text": "Fernando Eimbcke", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/person/details/202142/fernando-eimbcke"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ihr Film erzählt von einem kleinen Jungen und seinem Vater. Auf welche filmischen Vorbilder haben sie dabei zurückgegriffen?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Eimbcke : Ganz wichtig war „ The Kid “ (1921) von Charlie Chaplin. Chaplin ist eines der größten Genies der Filmgeschichte. Er hat mich als Filmemacher sehr beeinflusst. Chaplin schafft es immer wieder, zwei sehr unterschiedliche Genres zu verschmelzen: das Drama und die Komödie. Auf der einen Seite gibt es diese dramatische Übersteigerung in seinen Filmen, in der eigentlich alle Figuren nur noch Opfer sind; auf der anderen Seite findet sich ein brachialer Humor, bei dem Sahnetorten in die Gesichter klatschen. Es ist ein Drama, aber der Grundton ist dennoch realistisch, daher auch der Begriff Neorealismus. Ich glaube, wenn man sich beim Erzählen auf die Wirklichkeit stützen kann, ist das eine sehr starke Basis. Aber man muss sich dieser Wirklichkeit öffnen, sich ihr anpassen und darf nicht versuchen, die Wirklichkeit an sich anzupassen.", "links": [{"text": "Fahrraddiebe", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/film/details/27637/fahrraddiebe"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/bild/filmdb/380405/fernando-eimbcke-moscas.jpg?t=1792578752", "alt": "Fernando Eimbcke bei der Berlinale 2026 ", "caption": "Fernando Eimbcke bei der Berlinale 2026 (© imago/Funke Foto Service)", "credit": "Filmdienst"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Wie haben Sie diese Einflüsse von Chaplin und dem italienischen Neorealismus in Ihre eigene Filmsprache übersetzt?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Eimbcke : Gemeinsam mit der Drehbuchautorin Vanesa Garnica habe ich den Spannungsbogen für „Moscas“ entwickelt. Wir ließen die Straße einfach so leben, wie sie lebte. Wir haben nicht auffällig gefilmt, Straßen gesperrt und Lastwagen aufgestellt, sondern die Kamera versteckt angebracht; wir waren dabei sehr diskret und haben nur mit einem sehr kleinen Filmteam gearbeitet. Ozu hat meine Arbeit bei den Innenaufnahmen stark beeinflusst. Allerdings drehte er nur ungern im Freien, da er dort das Gefühl hatte, die Kontrolle über die Inszenierung zu verlieren. Bei „Moscas“ verfolge ich bewusst einen entgegengesetzten Ansatz. Ich wollte auf der Straße drehen, um die Kontrolle ein Stück weit aufzugeben. Tatsächlich haben wir das Krankenhaus bis ins Detail studiert und wollten wissen, wie alles aussieht und funktioniert – die Maschinenräume ebenso wie die Krankenzimmer.
